check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, clear introduction, confirms identity, explains the purpose of the consultation, and asks consent for a breast examination with a chaperone offered.
Empathic, non-judgemental approach, including when discussing smoking; uses plain language without jargon.
History
Characterises the lump and the infection:

kids.x: Onset, duration, change in size, pain, redness.
Response to antibiotics so far, adherence and allergies.

check.x: Establishes that this is non-lactational: asks about breastfeeding, pregnancy and last menstrual period.
Asks about breast cancer symptoms and risk factors:

kids.x: Nipple retraction or discharge, skin changes, previous similar episode.
Weight loss, bone pain, respiratory symptoms.
Family history of breast and ovarian cancer, previous imaging or biopsy, hormone use.

check.x: Asks about smoking, diabetes and other risk factors for recurrent periductal infection.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations, including her fear of cancer and her reluctance to have tests.
Examination
Asks for observations (temperature, heart rate, blood pressure) and looks for signs of sepsis.
Inspects both breasts, sitting with arms by her sides and then raised:
Palpates both breasts, the normal side first, including the retroareolar region, and describes the mass: size, consistency, fixity to skin and a fluctuant centre.
Examines the axillary, supraclavicular and cervical lymph nodes on both sides.
Briefly checks the chest, liver and spine for signs of spread, given the suspicion of malignancy.
Interpretation
Bloods: raised white cell count, neutrophilia and CRP in keeping with bacterial infection; normal HbA1c, so no diabetes.
Ultrasound: an abscess suitable for aspiration with a separate irregular solid mass beneath it that is suspicious for malignancy, plus an indeterminate axillary node.
Mammogram: suspicious left retroareolar mass with skin thickening and nipple retraction; right breast normal.

States that a non-lactational abscess that has not responded to antibiotics, with a persisting mass, may be caused by or may mask a carcinoma, including inflammatory breast cancer, and that cancer must be excluded.
Names the features that raise suspicion here: residual firm irregular mass, peau d'orange, nipple retraction, axillary node, recurrence at the same site, age over 40 and family history.
Management
Decides she is not septic and can be managed as an outpatient with close review, and states when she would need hospital referral.
Plans drainage of the abscess, with ultrasound-guided needle aspiration preferred to incision, and sends the pus for culture.
Plans tissue diagnosis now, not after the infection settles:

kids.x: Core biopsy (not FNA alone) of the solid mass and abscess wall.
Skin punch biopsy of the thickened skin if inflammatory breast cancer is suspected.
Biopsy of the indeterminate axillary node.

check.x: Explains the triple test (clinical, imaging and non-operative biopsy) and that all three must agree before the lump is called benign.
States that any discordance, or a persistent or recurrent lesion after treatment, needs further investigation and tissue diagnosis.
Reviews the antibiotic with eTG: non-lactational infection often needs anaerobic cover (for example amoxicillin with clavulanate), adjusted to the culture; advises analgesia.
Refers urgently to a breast surgeon or breast clinic.
Responds honestly to her fear of cancer:

kids.x: Acknowledges her concern and her friend's experience.
Says infection is part of the picture but the scans show a mass that must be tested for cancer; avoids both false reassurance and a premature diagnosis of cancer.

check.x: Explains why the biopsy is needed even though this looks like an infection, and what aspiration and core biopsy involve, addressing her reluctance about tests.
Offers smoking cessation support and notes smoking as a risk factor for periductal mastitis and recurrence.
Summarises the plan, checks understanding, confirms she agrees and invites questions.
Safety netting
Tells her to return the same day or go to the Emergency Department for spreading redness, worsening pain, high fever or rigors, vomiting, or feeling faint or very unwell.
Arranges review in 48 to 72 hours after drainage, with the culture result.
Arranges follow-up for the biopsy results with the breast team, and follows her until the mass has fully resolved, with repeat imaging or biopsy if any mass remains.

desc: This station involves a focused history and breast examination of a woman who is not breastfeeding and has a red, painful breast lump that has not settled on antibiotics, then interpreting her bloods, ultrasound and mammogram, planning drainage, tissue diagnosis and referral, and explaining why cancer must be excluded.
explain:
Why a non-lactational breast abscess is a red flag

Breast infection in a woman who is not breastfeeding is unusual. It may be periductal mastitis (strongly associated with smoking), but an infection can also be caused by, or can mask, an underlying carcinoma. Inflammatory breast cancer commonly mimics mastitis, with a red, warm, swollen breast, skin thickening and peau d'orange, and is often treated as an infection for weeks before it is recognised. Failure to respond to antibiotics, a residual mass, nipple retraction, an axillary node and recurrence at the same site all raise concern. Helen is 46, has a family history, has had a previous episode at the same site, and on examination has a firm, ill-defined retroareolar mass partly fixed to the skin, new nipple retraction, early peau d'orange and an axillary node.

Interpreting the results

  • Bloods: a raised white cell count, neutrophilia and CRP fit a bacterial infection. They do not exclude cancer. A normal HbA1c excludes undiagnosed diabetes as a contributor.

  • Ultrasound: the collection with debris is the abscess and can be aspirated under ultrasound. The separate irregular, vascular solid mass with angular margins is the finding that matters: it is suspicious for malignancy and needs a core biopsy. A node with a thickened cortex is indeterminate (it may be reactive to infection) and should be sampled.

  • Mammogram: at 35 or over, imaging is ultrasound plus mammogram. Here it shows a suspicious retroareolar mass with skin thickening and nipple retraction, and a normal right breast. Inflammation can limit the mammogram, which is another reason ultrasound and biopsy are essential.

What must be done, and when

  • Image at presentation, not after the infection settles, and assess the axilla.

  • Treat the infection: ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is preferred over incision and drainage, with pus sent for culture, and antibiotics chosen according to eTG (non-lactational infection often needs anaerobic cover).

  • Biopsy any residual mass, abscess wall or skin change. Core biopsy is preferred to FNA for a solid lesion. A skin punch biopsy is needed if inflammatory breast cancer is a possibility. Persistent or recurrent disease requires tissue diagnosis.

  • Refer urgently to a breast surgeon or breast clinic and review early (48 to 72 hours). Follow the patient until the mass has resolved completely.

Triple test

The three components are clinical assessment (history and examination of both breasts and axillae), imaging (age 35 or over: mammogram plus ultrasound; under 35: ultrasound first, with mammogram added selectively) and non-operative tissue biopsy (core biopsy preferred to FNA for solid lesions). The key rule is concordance: a lump can be called benign only if all three components agree. Any discordance, for example a benign-looking biopsy from a mass that is clinically or radiologically suspicious, needs further investigation, such as repeat or larger-volume biopsy, or excision.

Communication and safety netting

Patients are often reluctant to have more tests when they have been told it is an infection. Explain honestly that there is an infection, but that the scans show a separate lump that must be tested and that the only way to be certain is a biopsy. Avoid false reassurance, but also avoid telling her she has cancer before the results are available. Support smoking cessation. Tell her to return the same day or go to the Emergency Department for spreading redness, worsening pain, high fever, rigors or feeling very unwell, and make sure the biopsy results and her follow-up are booked.
focus: Breast lump and breast abscess work-up
guide:
In Part 1, the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. A high-performing candidate establishes that the lump is non-lactational, asks about cancer symptoms and risk factors, examines both breasts and all nodal areas with a chaperone offered, and in Part 2 recognises an abscess with a separate suspicious solid mass and an indeterminate node. They state clearly that malignancy, including inflammatory breast cancer, must be excluded, plan aspiration with culture and core biopsy now, explain the concordance rule of the triple test, refer urgently to a breast surgeon, and counsel her honestly with specific safety netting and follow-up until the mass has gone.

A borderline candidate treats this as simple mastitis, changes the antibiotic and arranges review without tissue diagnosis, or defers biopsy until the infection has resolved. They may miss the separate solid mass on the ultrasound report, omit the axilla in the examination, or give false reassurance when asked about cancer.
patient:
Role: You are Helen Marchetti, a 46-year-old primary school teacher. You are worried but trying to play it down. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine. Agree to a breast examination if the candidate explains it, asks your permission and offers a chaperone.

Opening line: "This lump in my breast is still sore and red, and the antibiotics don't seem to be doing much."

The lump and the infection (give only when asked):

  • Ten days ago you noticed a tender area near the left nipple. It has become a firm, red, painful lump. It has not shrunk.
  • You saw a locum GP five days ago, who said it was mastitis and gave you flucloxacillin 500 mg four times a day. You have taken every dose. The redness is a bit better but the lump is still there and feels hard.
  • Fevers and sweats on and off for four days. You feel tired. No rigors, no vomiting, no dizziness.
  • No trauma, nipple piercing or recent breast procedure.

Breastfeeding and pregnancy: You are not breastfeeding. Your youngest child is 12 and you last breastfed 11 years ago. You are not pregnant: periods are regular, last period 2 weeks ago.

Breast symptoms and past episodes:

  • No nipple discharge. The left nipple has been slightly pulled in for about a month; you thought it was nothing.
  • You had a similar, smaller sore area near the same nipple 18 months ago, which settled with antibiotics. No scan was done.
  • You have never had a mammogram, a breast biopsy or any breast imaging.
  • No weight loss, bone pain, cough, breathlessness or headaches.

Medical history: Nil significant. No diabetes. No regular medicines apart from the flucloxacillin. No hormonal contraception or HRT. No known drug allergies.

Family history: Your mother had breast cancer at 58. No ovarian cancer in the family. No one has had genetic testing.

Social history: You smoke 15 cigarettes a day and have for 25 years. Alcohol 2 standard drinks on weekends. Married, two children. You are busy at work and do not want to take time off.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: You think it is an infection that needs a stronger antibiotic. Underneath, you are frightened because a friend was told she had mastitis and it turned out to be cancer. You hope for a different antibiotic and to get back to work.

Things to say:

  • Early on: "I just want this infection gone. I haven't got time for lots of tests."
  • If there is time: "A friend of mine was told she had mastitis and it turned out to be cancer. Could that be what this is?" Settle if the candidate is honest and clear, without false reassurance or alarm.
points: Non-lactational breast abscess or mastitis is a red flag for underlying carcinoma, including inflammatory breast cancer, and needs imaging at presentation as well as treatment of the infection.
Women aged 35 or over need ultrasound plus mammogram; under 35, ultrasound first with selective mammogram.
Biopsy (core preferred over FNA) any residual mass, abscess wall or skin change; persistent or recurrent disease needs tissue diagnosis.
Triple assessment is clinical, imaging and non-operative biopsy, and all three must be concordant before a lump is called benign.
Follow the patient until the mass has completely resolved and do not give false reassurance.

stem: You are a final-year medical student on a General Practice placement. Helen Marchetti, a 46-year-old woman, has come back to the clinic because a painful, red lump in her left breast has not settled on the antibiotics a locum GP started five days ago.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mrs Marchetti and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her blood results and the reports of her breast ultrasound and mammogram. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, including what you would explain to Mrs Marchetti, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
title: Non-lactational breast abscess

part2.lead: Mrs Marchetti had blood tests, a bilateral mammogram and an ultrasound of the left breast and axilla at the imaging centre next door this afternoon. She has come back to see you. Here are the results.

handover.label: Bloods (today)
handover.model:
• Read: neutrophilia (white cells 13.6, neutrophils 10.8) and a CRP of 58, with normal haemoglobin and platelets. HbA1c 5.3% (34 mmol/mol) is normal; 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more would diagnose diabetes.
  • For Mrs Marchetti: a bacterial infection with a systemic response, in keeping with the abscess and her low-grade fever. With a normal blood pressure, an alert patient and only a mild fever she is not septic. The normal HbA1c rules out undiagnosed diabetes as a contributor.
  • What it changes: she can be treated as an outpatient with drainage, antibiotics and close review, and these values are the baseline for that review. Inflammatory markers cannot tell infection from cancer: a raised CRP does not explain away the mass.

handover.label: Ultrasound of the left breast and axilla
handover.result:
Examination: ultrasound of the left breast and left axilla, targeted to the clinical lump.

Clinical details: 46-year-old woman, not lactating. Tender, red left retroareolar lump for 10 days, not settling after 5 days of flucloxacillin. Left nipple retraction for one month. Smoker. Mother had breast cancer at 58. Similar episode at the same site 18 months ago.

Comparison: no previous breast imaging.

Findings:

  • Left breast, retroareolar, extending to 10 to 11 o'clock, 0 to 3 cm from the nipple: a 26 × 22 × 18 mm collection (about 5 mL) with a thick (3 mm) wall, mobile internal debris, hyperaemia of the wall on Doppler and no internal flow, in keeping with an abscess.
  • Left breast, 10 o'clock, 2 cm from the nipple, deep to the collection and separate from it: a 21 × 16 × 14 mm hypoechoic solid mass, irregular in shape, with angular, indistinct margins and posterior acoustic shadowing. Internal vascularity on Doppler. It does not change with probe pressure.
  • Skin: thickened to 6 mm over the lump (normal up to 2 mm), with oedema of the subcutaneous fat.
  • Remainder of the left breast: no other focal lesion.
  • Left axilla: one 15 × 9 mm level 1 lymph node with eccentric cortical thickening to 5 mm and a preserved fatty hilum. The other level 1 nodes look normal.

Synoptic categories: collection 2 (benign: abscess); solid mass 4 (suspicious of malignancy); axillary node 3 (indeterminate).

Conclusion: left retroareolar abscess suitable for ultrasound-guided aspiration, with a separate underlying solid mass suspicious for malignancy (category 4) and an indeterminate left axillary node (category 3). Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the mass and sampling of the node recommended; correlate with mammography.
handover.model:
• Read: two separate lesions. The thick-walled collection with mobile debris and a hyperaemic wall is the abscess, small enough (about 5 mL) to aspirate. Deep to it is a solid mass with the features of cancer: irregular shape, angular, indistinct margins, shadowing, internal vascularity and no change with compression (category 4). Skin thickening of 6 mm means oedema, from inflammation or from tumour in the dermal lymphatics. The node has a cortex of 5 mm (more than 3 mm is abnormal) but a preserved hilum: indeterminate, reactive or metastatic.
  • For Mrs Marchetti: infection is part of the picture, but a separate suspicious mass means a possible underlying carcinoma, including inflammatory breast cancer, that must be proved or excluded now.
  • What it changes: ultrasound-guided aspiration of the abscess with pus sent for culture, and ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the mass and sampling of the node at the same time, not after the infection settles; urgent referral to a breast surgeon or breast clinic.

handover.label: Bilateral diagnostic mammogram
handover.result:
Examination: bilateral diagnostic mammogram, craniocaudal and mediolateral oblique views. Compression of the left breast was limited by tenderness.

Clinical details: as for the ultrasound; suspected left breast abscess not responding to antibiotics, with nipple retraction.

Comparison: no previous mammograms.

Breast composition: heterogeneously dense (ACR category C), which may obscure small lesions.

Findings:

  • Left: an ill-defined, irregular retroareolar density about 40 mm across, extending into the upper inner quadrant, with retraction of the nipple, skin thickening over the inner breast and coarse trabecular markings in keeping with oedema. No suspicious calcifications. A dense lymph node is partly included at the edge of the left axilla on the oblique view.
  • Right: no mass, architectural distortion or suspicious calcification. Skin and nipple normal.

Synoptic categories: left 4 (suspicious of malignancy); right 1 (no significant abnormality).

Conclusion: left retroareolar mass with skin thickening and nipple retraction, suspicious of malignancy (category 4); correlate with the ultrasound and tissue sampling. Right breast normal (category 1).
handover.model:
• Read: dense breasts (category C), which lowers the sensitivity of the mammogram. On the left an irregular retroareolar mass about 40 mm across (the abscess and the solid mass together) with nipple retraction, skin thickening and oedema, and a dense axillary node; no calcifications, which does not exclude cancer. The right breast is normal.
  • For Mrs Marchetti: the mammogram agrees with the examination and the ultrasound: a suspicious left mass (category 4), with features that fit inflammatory or underlying carcinoma as well as infection. A normal right breast is reassuring for that side only.
  • What it changes: at 46 she needs mammogram plus ultrasound, and both are now suspicious, so the imaging arm of the triple test is suspicious. Tissue diagnosis is needed now, and a benign biopsy result would be discordant and need repeat or larger-volume biopsy or excision.

ask: You are now calling the breast surgical registrar at the local hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Mrs Marchetti, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Mrs Marchetti now, here in general practice.
Before Mrs Marchetti goes home, what would you tell her and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, final-year student at the GP clinic; Helen Marchetti, 46.
  • Situation: left breast abscess not settling after 5 days of flucloxacillin, with a separate suspicious mass. She is not septic.
  • Background: not breastfeeding. Lump for 10 days, nipple retraction for 1 month, same site 18 months ago. Smokes 15 a day. Mother had breast cancer at 58. No allergies.
  • Assessment: WCC 13.6, neutrophils 10.8, CRP 58: bacterial infection. HbA1c 5.3%: no diabetes. Ultrasound: abscess of about 5 mL, can be aspirated. Separate irregular vascular solid mass (category 4), skin 6 mm thick, axillary node with a 5 mm cortex (indeterminate). Mammogram: left mass category 4, right normal. Possible underlying carcinoma, including inflammatory.
  • Recommendation: urgent breast clinic within days for aspiration with culture, core biopsy of the mass, node sampling and skin punch biopsy.

Most likely: non-lactational left breast abscess. For it: fever, tender red lump, WCC and CRP raised, thick-walled collection with debris. Carcinoma must be excluded.

  • Underlying carcinoma or inflammatory breast cancer: for it: no response to antibiotics, a separate irregular vascular solid mass (category 4), peau d'orange, skin thickening, new nipple retraction, indeterminate node, recurrence at the same site, age 46, mother affected. No tissue diagnosis yet.
  • Periductal mastitis: for it: heavy smoker, retroareolar site, recurrence. Against it: does not explain the separate solid mass.
  • Lactational mastitis or abscess: excluded. She last breastfed 11 years ago and is not pregnant. That makes this non-lactational, which is a red flag for cancer.

1. Disposition: not septic, so treat as an outpatient. Refer to hospital if signs of sepsis, rapidly spreading cellulitis or no improvement.
  2. Urgent referral: phone a breast surgeon or breast clinic today.
  3. Drainage: ultrasound-guided needle aspiration rather than incision. Send the pus for culture.
  4. Tissue diagnosis now, not after the infection settles: core biopsy (not FNA alone) of the mass and abscess wall, sampling of the axillary node, and skin punch biopsy for possible inflammatory cancer.
  5. Triple test: clinical, imaging and biopsy must all agree before calling it benign. A benign biopsy here would be discordant and needs repeat or larger biopsy, or excision.
  6. Antibiotics (eTG): change to amoxicillin with clavulanate 875/125 mg orally 12-hourly for anaerobic cover. Adjust to the culture. Paracetamol or an NSAID for pain.
  7. Smoking cessation support (Quitline, NRT).

• Honest explanation: acknowledge her fear and her friend's experience. There is an infection, but the scans show a separate lump that must be tested. A biopsy is the only way to be sure. Avoid false reassurance and avoid saying it is cancer.
  • The tests: needle drainage and core biopsy under ultrasound with local anaesthetic, usually in one visit.
  • Red flags (same day to GP or go to ED): spreading redness, worsening pain, high fever or shaking chills, vomiting, feeling faint or very unwell.
  • Follow-up: GP review 48 to 72 hours after drainage, with the culture result. Biopsy results given in person with the breast team, and she can bring a support person. Follow her until the mass has fully gone, with repeat imaging or biopsy if any mass remains.
